clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, typically pure spastic paraplegia caused by variants in WASHC5, which encodes strumpellin, a component of the endosomal WASH complex
Presentation is usually adult-onset with progressive lower-limb spasticity, weakness and urinary urgency
SPG8 is often described as relatively severe and comparatively rapidly progressive within the pure HSP group
Reduced vibration sense at the ankles is common, but overt sensory ataxia is unusual
Strumpellin participates in actin-mediated endosomal sorting and recycling, tying SPG8 to intracellular trafficking defects
Diagnosis rests on gene-panel testing once acquired myelopathies have been excluded
Treatment is symptomatic, with physiotherapy, spasticity control, orthoses and bladder management
reference.pathophysiology: SPG8 is caused by heterozygous variants in WASHC5, the gene for strumpellin, a scaffolding subunit of the WASH (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homologue) complex. This complex nucleates branched actin on endosomal membranes to drive sorting and recycling of receptors and other cargo. Disruption of strumpellin impairs endosomal trafficking and membrane homeostasis within neurons, and the longest corticospinal axons are especially dependent on efficient cargo handling. The resulting distal axonopathy underlies the progressive, often relatively severe spastic paraparesis characteristic of SPG8.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 and other pure autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegias
Multiple sclerosis with a progressive spinal course
Vitamin B12 or copper deficiency myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: WASHC5 sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel
MRI of brain and whole spine to exclude structural and demyelinating disease
Nerve conduction studies and evoked potentials to characterise long-tract involvement
Vitamin B12, copper and metabolic myelopathy screen
Family assessment to confirm the dominant pattern
redFlags: Rapid loss of ambulation prompting exclusion of a treatable structural cause
A distinct sensory level suggesting an acquired myelopathy
Bulbar involvement or fasciculations raising concern for motor neurone disease
Acute urinary retention requiring urgent assessment
reference.prognosis: SPG8 is generally slowly progressive but is regarded as one of the more disabling pure hereditary spastic paraplegias, and a proportion of patients need walking aids within one to two decades of onset.
pitfalls: Assuming all pure HSP is slowly progressive and delaying supportive input in a more aggressive SPG8 course
Failing to exclude a compressive myelopathy before attributing symptoms to a genetic cause
Overlooking WASHC5 on smaller gene panels focused on the commonest loci
Misinterpreting mild sensory signs as evidence against hereditary spastic paraplegia
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying treatment is available; reduce spasticity with oral agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, focal botulinum toxin for spastic muscles, and consider intrathecal baclofen in severe disability
Structured physiotherapy with stretching, strengthening, ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids to maintain gait and prevent contractures
Manage the characteristic urinary urgency with antimuscarinic therapy, urodynamic assessment and continence support
Occupational therapy and home-adaptation input given the comparatively rapid, disabling progression of this subtype
Surveillance of walking capacity, falls risk and bladder function to time provision of aids and interventions
Multidisciplinary follow-up across neurology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthotics
Offer genetic counselling and predictive testing of relatives, reflecting autosomal dominant inheritance of WASHC5 variants
